subject: pathology
title: Oral cavity and salivary glands: lesions and tumours

steps.tx: Evaluating oral white patches requires distinguishing reactive lesions from premalignant **oral leukoplakia**, defined as a clinical white plaque that cannot be scraped off or characterized as another disease entity. Biopsy is essential because histological examination grades epithelial dysplasia from hyperkeratosis to carcinoma in situ. Non-homogeneous, speckled or verrucous leukoplakias carry higher malignant transformation rates than thin homogeneous plaques. Erythroplakia, a velvety red plaque, carries an even higher risk, with severe dysplasia or carcinoma found in most biopsies. Oral lichen planus produces characteristic bilateral reticular Wickham striae.
steps.say: Oral leukoplakia is a clinical white patch on the oral mucosa that cannot be scraped off or attributed to another specific disease entity. Biopsy is essential because histological examination may reveal epithelial dysplasia, which carries a tangible risk of malignant transformation. Non homogeneous or speckled lesions carry a much higher likelihood of dysplasia than flat homogeneous plaques. Erythroplakia is an intense velvety red patch that is far more ominous, demonstrating severe dysplasia or invasive malignancy in most cases. Suspicious oral lesions lasting several weeks warrant mandatory incisional biopsy.

steps.tx: Over ninety percent of oral malignancies are **oral squamous cell carcinoma**, driven by synergistic carcinogen exposure from tobacco smoking, betel quid with areca nut, and alcohol. High-risk human papillomavirus genotype sixteen increasingly causes oropharyngeal cancers in younger individuals. Common anatomical sites include the ventrolateral tongue border and floor of the mouth, typically presenting as non-healing ulcers with indurated, everted edges. Field cancerization explains why patients remain at lifelong risk of developing synchronous or metachronous secondary primary tumors across the aerodigestive tract following chronic mucosal carcinogen exposure.
steps.say: Squamous cell carcinoma accounts for more than ninety percent of all oral malignancies, commonly arising on the lateral border of the tongue and the floor of the mouth. Chronic exposure to tobacco, alcohol and betel quid acts synergistically to induce genetic mutations in the mucosal epithelium, while human papillomavirus type sixteen drives many oropharyngeal cancers. Lesions typically present as painless, non healing ulcers with firm indurated edges or fungating masses. Because carcinogens expose the entire mucosal lining, field cancerization frequently causes multiple synchronous primary tumours throughout the upper aerodigestive tract.

steps.tx: The commonest benign salivary neoplasm is **pleomorphic adenoma**, also called mixed tumor due to its biphasic histology mixing ductal epithelial elements with myxoid, chondroid and hyaline stroma. It arises characteristically in the superficial parotid gland as a slow-growing, painless, firm, mobile mass in middle age. Treatment requires superficial parotidectomy with facial nerve preservation; simple enucleation or capsular rupture spills microscopic pseudopods, causing multifocal recurrence. Long-standing untreated tumors risk malignant transformation into aggressive carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma, signaled by sudden rapid growth, pain or facial paralysis.
steps.say: Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common benign salivary gland neoplasm, most frequently encountered as a slow growing, painless, mobile lump in the superficial parotid gland. Histological examination reveals a remarkable biphasic mixture of epithelial ductal structures surrounded by chondromyxoid or hyaline stroma. Treatment requires superficial parotidectomy with careful preservation of the facial nerve branches. Simple enucleation must be avoided because tumour pseudopods penetrate the fibrous pseudocapsule, leading to troublesome multifocal recurrences if the capsule ruptures. An old indolent lump that rapidly enlarges suggests malignant transformation into carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma.

steps.tx: The most frequent salivary gland malignancy is **mucoepidermoid carcinoma**, composed of a variable mixture of mucin-producing, intermediate and squamoid epithelial cells, graded histologically into low, intermediate and high grades that dictate prognosis. In contrast, adenoid cystic carcinoma arises commonly in minor salivary glands and submandibular glands, exhibiting classic cribriform swiss-cheese nests of basaloid cells. A hallmark of adenoid cystic carcinoma is extensive perineural invasion causing early severe pain, followed by late hematogenous metastases to lungs and bones despite infrequent regional lymph node involvement.
steps.say: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma represents the most common primary salivary gland malignancy, featuring a characteristic mixture of squamoid, intermediate and mucin producing epithelial cells. Clinical outcome correlates closely with histological grading from low to high grade cancers. Adenoid cystic carcinoma is recognized by classic cribriform or swiss cheese nests of basaloid cells. It has an extraordinary propensity for perineural invasion, causing early pain and nerve palsy. Although lymph node spread is uncommon, adenoid cystic carcinoma frequently produces relentless late pulmonary metastases.

steps.tx: Salivary disorders include acute bacterial sialadenitis, mumps parotitis, obstructive sialolithiasis and autoimmune destruction. Sjogren syndrome produces autoimmune destruction of salivary and lacrimal glands, with lymphocytic infiltration causing xerostomia and keratoconjunctivitis sicca. Longstanding Sjogren syndrome carries a marked risk of developing extranodal marginal zone B-cell **MALT lymphoma** within affected glands. Persistent, asymmetric or firm parotid enlargement in these patients demands prompt biopsy. Obstructive sialolithiasis most frequently affects the submandibular Wharton duct, causing recurrent colicky pain and swelling during meals from mechanical obstruction of salivary flow.
steps.say: Salivary gland enlargement can stem from mechanical obstruction, bacterial infection or chronic autoimmune inflammation. Bacterial sialadenitis typically affects dehydrated elderly patients when reduced salivary flow allows oral flora to infect the gland. Sialolithiasis forms stones in the submandibular Wharton duct, causing mealtime pain and swelling. Sjogren syndrome leads to autoimmune destruction of salivary tissue with lymphocytic infiltrates. Crucially, longstanding Sjogren disease predisposes to extranodal MALT lymphoma, meaning persistent firm glandular enlargement requires prompt histological biopsy to exclude malignancy.
